body:
Why marketing support is a make-or-break question

Every brokerage recruiting pitch mentions marketing support. Almost none of them define it the same way. For one office, “marketing support” means a template you can edit yourself in a design app. For another, it means a dedicated staff photographer, a built-in personal website, and social content ready to post. The gap between those two experiences is enormous, and it directly affects how much you spend out of pocket and how professional your first listings look. Before you sign with any brokerage, it’s worth slowing down and comparing what’s actually offered, not what’s implied.

Does the brokerage give you a personal website or landing page?

A personal website or agent landing page is one of the most useful things a brokerage can provide, because building one yourself takes time and money you may not have as a new agent. Ask directly: is a personal page included as part of joining, does it come pre-populated with your listings and contact information, and can you customize it, or is it a generic template that looks identical to every other agent’s page? Some offices include this at no extra cost. Others charge a monthly fee for it, and some don’t offer one at all, leaving you to build your own site or landing page from scratch.

Will you get professional photography and listing marketing help?

Good photos sell listings faster, and professional photography is one of the clearest signals of real marketing support. Ask whether the brokerage provides or subsidizes professional photography for your listings, whether that includes basic staging guidance, and whether there’s support for listing flyers, brochures, or virtual tour setup. Some brokerages have a photographer on staff or a preferred vendor at a reduced rate. Others expect you to hire and pay for photography entirely on your own for every listing, which adds up quickly when you’re just getting started.

Are the social media templates something you’ll actually use?

Almost every brokerage will point to social media templates as part of their marketing package. The real question is whether they’re genuinely usable. Ask to see the actual templates: are they easy to customize with your own photo and contact details, do they look current, and are they something agents realistically post week to week, or do they sit unused because they’re clunky or off-brand? A stack of templates nobody opens isn’t marketing support, it’s a line item in a slide deck.

How much of your marketing budget will you be funding yourself?

Even at brokerages with strong support, some marketing spend usually falls to you. It could be paid ads, print mailers, a booth at a local event, or a premium version of a tool the brokerage offers a basic version of. Ask specifically what’s included at no cost, what’s offered at a discount, and what you’re expected to pay for entirely on your own. Getting concrete numbers or ranges before you join lets you budget realistically for your first year instead of being surprised by costs after you’ve already signed on.

The single best way to know: ask to see it, not hear about it

The most reliable way to evaluate marketing support is to ask for real examples from real agents. Request to see an actual agent’s personal website, a real listing flyer or postcard that went out recently, and the social templates agents are using that month. A recruiting conversation can describe a tool that technically exists but barely gets used, or that looks impressive in a slide but clunky in practice. Seeing the real thing, and hearing directly from an agent who uses it, tells you far more than any features list.

What this means for your first year

The marketing support a brokerage provides, or doesn’t, shapes your first year more than most new agents expect. Strong support means you can focus your time and money on building relationships and generating leads instead of building a website or hunting for a photographer. Thin support means those costs and that time come out of your own pocket from day one. Neither is automatically wrong, but you should know which situation you’re walking into before you sign, so you can plan your budget and your time accordingly.

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been Daytona Beach’s largest brokerage since 1963, and part of what that scale provides is real marketing infrastructure behind agents, not just a slide about it. If you’re comparing brokerages and want to see actual examples of the websites, photography, and social tools agents use here, start a conversation and we’ll show you the real thing.

There is a quieter question hiding inside marketing support, which is who actually owns the listing photography once you stop working there.

faq.q: What marketing support should a real estate brokerage provide new agents?
faq.a: At minimum, ask about a personal website or landing page, access to professional photography for listings, and social media templates or content you can actually use. How much of each is included versus self-funded varies a lot by brokerage, so get specifics before you join.

faq.q: Is it normal to pay for my own real estate marketing?
faq.a: Yes, to some degree. Most agents fund at least part of their own marketing, especially personal branding and lead generation beyond what the brokerage provides. The key question isn't whether you'll spend anything, it's how much of the basics (photography, a web presence, templates) the brokerage covers versus leaves entirely to you.

faq.q: How do I find out what marketing support is really like at a brokerage?
faq.a: Ask to see actual examples: a current agent's personal website, a real listing flyer, or the social media templates agents use week to week. A features list in a recruiting conversation can describe something that barely gets used in practice, so real examples are the most reliable evidence.

faq.q: Does a bigger brokerage always mean better marketing support?
faq.a: Not automatically. Size can mean more resources, but it can also mean generic, one-size-fits-all tools. What matters more is whether the marketing support fits how you'll actually work, and whether current agents at that office are genuinely using and benefiting from it.
